literature.note: full force field + backrub sampling, model-averaged (Barlow 2018)

verdict: On the field-standard metrics, our node reaches Pearson 0.471 / Spearman 0.479 / RMSE 1.25 kcal/mol / AUC 0.764 for classifying destabilising interface mutations, on a HARD complex-held-out split of 2602 alanine-scan mutations. Placed against published SKEMPI benchmarks: Rosetta flex_ddG is the accuracy leader at Pearson ~0.63 (full force field + backrub sampling, model-averaged, minutes-to-hours per mutation); FoldX ~0.48 and Rosetta cartesian_ddg ~0.50 (seconds-to-a-minute); mCSM-PPI2 ~0.58 blind (its ~0.75 CV number is inflated by train/test similarity). So our reduced node lands around FoldX / cartesian_ddg territory and reaches roughly 75% of flex_ddG's correlation — while running in ~2 ms/mutation, i.e. ~10^4-10^6x faster than flex_ddG. CRITICAL CAVEAT — do NOT read our lower RMSE (1.25 vs ~1.5) as beating Rosetta: our alanine subset has a NARROW ΔΔG spread (the mean-predictor RMSE is already 1.37), so a low RMSE mostly reflects the test distribution, not accuracy; Pearson is the only fair cross-benchmark metric here, and on Pearson Rosetta leads. This is also NOT a head-to-head — different mutation subset, and our complex-held-out split is HARDER than the splits several published numbers use (so like-for-like our gap to Rosetta may be smaller than it looks, and mCSM's CV number is not comparable at all). Bottom line: Rosetta wins on accuracy, as expected from decades of force-field + sampling engineering; our node is a fast TRIAGE predictor at ~FoldX accuracy and a tiny fraction of the compute — useful for ranking many variants, not for a final energy. The honest way to close the gap is rotamer sampling + a real electrostatics/solvation term.
